Copies overlap only if both source buffers are in the same pinned allocation
One H2D copy at a time, but a copy can overlap with a kernel
explain: The best practices guide ties this to asyncEngineCount: a GPU with one copy engine can perform one transfer and execute kernels concurrently, while two copy engines additionally allow a host to device and a device to host transfer at the same time. Streams give permission to overlap; the engine count caps how much overlap the hardware can deliver.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
question: A team wants to replace their bi-encoder with a cross-encoder for first-stage retrieval over 20 million passages. What is the core problem?
options: Cross-encoders cannot handle passages longer than a sentence
Every query would need 20 million transformer forward passes, because no document computation can be done ahead of time
Cross-encoders need the documents to be pre-embedded with the same model first
Cross-encoders only work with BM25 candidates
explain: The cross-encoder's document token states depend on the query, so nothing can be precomputed. Scoring a full corpus means one forward pass per document per query, which is why it is used only on a shortlist from a first stage.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Training a reranker: pointwise, pairwise, listwise and hard negatives
question: In the listwise softmax view, which candidate in our group receives the largest gradient pushing its score down?
options: The easy negative at -4.0
The positive at 2.0
The hard negative at 1.5
All negatives receive equal gradient
explain: For softmax cross-entropy the gradient on each negative's logit is its probability: 0.331 for z = 1.5, 0.122 for 0.5 and 0.001 for the easy one. The loss focuses on whichever negatives currently compete with the positive.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Encoding, hashing and encryption are three different things
question: A colleague stores API tokens Base64-encoded in the database "so they are not in plain text". What does an attacker who dumps the table need to use the tokens?
options: The encryption key from the application server
A large brute-force search of the token space
Nothing beyond a Base64 decoder, which every language ships
The hash salt
explain: Base64 is an encoding with no key. Decoding is instant and public. The tokens are effectively stored in plain text.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Authenticated encryption: AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and nonce reuse
question: A service encrypts with AES-GCM but uses a fixed nonce of 12 zero bytes for every message. What is lost?
options: Nothing, because GCM authenticates every message
Only the secrecy of the first message
Confidentiality of messages that share the nonce, and the ability to trust any tag under that key
Only performance
explain: Repeated nonce means repeated keystream (plaintext XORs leak) and, per SP 800-38D Appendix A, likely recovery of the hash subkey, which lets an attacker forge tags. Both secrecy and integrity fail.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Password hashing and key derivation: slow on purpose
question: Why is a per-user random salt essential even with a slow hash?
options: It makes each hash faster to verify
It replaces the need for a slow hash
Without it, users with the same password share a hash, so one guess tests all of them and precomputed tables work
It encrypts the password
explain: Salts make every user's hash unique, forcing the attacker to attack each account separately and defeating precomputation. Slowness then multiplies the cost of each separate attack.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Elliptic curves and digital signatures: the PS3 and CurveBall
question: Two ECDSA signatures from the same key have the same r value. What does that tell you?
options: Nothing; r often repeats
The messages were identical
The same per-message secret k was used, and the private key can be computed from the two signatures
The curve is broken
explain: r is the x-coordinate of kG, so equal r means equal k (for practical purposes). Then the two s equations solve for k and the private key, as with the PS3.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Layout algebra: composition, tiling and partitioning
question: In the CuTe GEMM tutorial, a CTA calls local_tile(mA, tiler, coord) and each thread then calls local_partition(gA, tA, threadIdx.x). What does each call keep?
options: local_tile keeps the tile mode and slices the rest; local_partition slices the tile mode and keeps the rest
Both keep the tile mode
local_tile keeps the rest mode; local_partition keeps the tile mode
Both keep the rest mode
explain: local_tile (inner partition) indexes the rest mode with the CTA coordinate and keeps one whole tile. local_partition (outer partition) indexes inside the tile with the thread index and keeps the repeats, so a thread gets one element per repeat of the thread tile.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
question: A host has all 64 cores rented to VMs and 100 GB of DRAM still free. Which statement is correct?
options: The 100 GB is stranded: no core is left to pair with it, so it cannot be rented until a VM leaves
The 100 GB is fine: the next VM to arrive can use it
The 100 GB will be swapped out to free space for other hosts
The 100 GB is lost only if the host is a NUMA machine
explain: VMs need cores and memory together. With zero free cores, no new VM fits on this host, so the free DRAM is paid for but unsellable. That is the definition of stranded memory that motivates pooling.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
question: With demotion enabled, a server's local DRAM node hits its low watermark. What happens to a cold anonymous page that would previously have gone to swap?
options: It is migrated to the CXL node and stays mapped, so a later access is a slower load rather than a page-in from disk
It is compressed into zswap on the local node
It is dropped and re-read from the executable file
It is moved to the CXL node but unmapped until a page fault brings it back to DRAM
explain: Demotion uses page migration in the reclaim path: the page moves to the next slower tier and the page tables are updated. The program can still load it directly, just with CXL latency.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Van Buren (2021): gates up or down, not good or bad motives
question: Why did the Court mention 'damage' and 'loss' when reading the statute?
options: Both focus on technological harms to data and systems, which fits a law aimed at hacking, not at misuse of information people may legitimately see
They prove Van Buren caused USD 5,000 of loss
They define the purpose test the government wanted
They only apply to civil cases, so they are irrelevant
explain: The opinion reasons from the statute's structure: the civil remedy's definitions of damage and loss address technological harm, which would be 'ill fitted' to remedying misuse of information employees permissibly access.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Writing and selling tools: Marcus Hutchins and dual-use code
question: Why is a sinkhole log sensitive even though it only contains infected machines' IP addresses?
options: IP addresses are encrypted keys
It identifies victims, who can be located and exploited by others before they clean up
It contains the malware's source code
It is not sensitive at all
explain: A list of infected addresses is a list of vulnerable, compromised machines. Shared with network owners and CERTs it speeds clean-up; published openly it is a target list. It is also personal data under laws such as the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation, the EU's data protection law).

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Evidence in court: authenticity, hearsay and chain of custody
question: In the hash-chained log, why does editing entry 1 also break entry 2's seal?
options: Because entry 2's seal is computed over entry 2 plus entry 1's seal
Because SHA-256 is slow
Because entry 2 was also edited
Because JSON sorting changed
explain: Each seal includes the previous seal. Change any entry and its seal changes, which changes the input to every later seal. Only rewriting all later seals hides the edit, which is why seals must be stored out of the editor's reach.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Why the pretraining mixture is a decision you cannot skip
question: A team doubles the weight of Wikipedia in a fixed 100B-token run. What must also happen?
options: Other domains must lose weight, because the weights sum to 1 and the token budget is fixed
Nothing else changes, because Wikipedia is a small domain
The run must be extended so the other domains keep their token counts
The tokenizer must be retrained for the new mixture
explain: Domain weights are a probability vector over a fixed budget. Raising one weight necessarily lowers others, so every reweighting is a trade, and the interesting question is whether a trade can help everything (lesson 4 shows it can).

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Upweighting means repeating: epochs, data limits and domain weights
question: DoReMi assigns 5 percent to a domain with 1B unique tokens, and you plan a 2T-token run. What happens, and what should you do?
options: Nothing: 5 percent is a small weight, so the domain cannot be over-read
The domain is read 10 times, which is fine because repeated data is as good as new
The domain is read 100 times, worth about 16 fresh passes by Muennighoff et al.'s fit; cap it near 4 epochs (weight 0.002) and give the rest to domains with unique data left
Drop the domain, because any repetition hurts the model
explain: 0.05 x 2T = 100B tokens from a 1B-token domain: 100 epochs. The fit gives an effective size of about 16.4 units for 100 read, so most of that compute is wasted. Capping at 4 epochs keeps 4B tokens (weight 0.002). Some repetition is fine, so dropping the domain throws away useful data.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Cleaning the crawl: heuristic rules, perplexity filters, exact dedup
question: Two pages share 85 percent of their shingles (Jaccard 0.85). Their MinHash signatures are split into 20 bands of 5 hashes; a pair becomes a candidate if all 5 minimums agree in at least one band. How likely is it that they are compared?
options: About 44 percent, the chance one band matches
About 85 percent, the Jaccard similarity itself
About 5 percent
Over 99.99 percent
explain: One band matches with probability 0.85 to the 5th = 0.444. All 20 bands miss with probability (1 - 0.444) to the 20th, about 8 in a million, so the pair is compared with probability 1 - 0.000008, over 99.99 percent. Banding turns a moderate per-band chance into near certainty for very similar pairs.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: SIMD lanes: contiguous loads, gathers, and blocked SoA
question: You vectorize `sum += pts[i].x` over AoS `Point {float x, y, z;}` with 8-wide AVX. What does the ISPC guide say the compiler must do to load eight x values?
options: A gather (or one scalar load per lane on CPUs without gather), because the x values are 12 bytes apart
One aligned 32-byte vector load
Nothing special: the cache line already holds all eight x values
Convert the array to SoA automatically at compile time
explain: The x values sit at offsets 0, 12, ..., 84, not adjacent, so a single contiguous load cannot fill the register. The guide says such an access "accesses non-sequential memory locations", so a gather is required. They also span 2 cache lines, not 1.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Seeing security from the data's side: copies, states and stages
question: In the Pegasus case, which finding shows the bucket held more than personal data?
options: It contained over 1.6 million crew files
It was open from February 2022
It was fixed three weeks after notification
Its source code contained plain-text passwords and secret keys, which could unlock other systems
explain: Credentials in a leaked bucket extend the exposure beyond the bucket itself: SafetyDetectives warned the keys could let someone tamper with flight data. Personal data and dates matter, but they do not show the leak reaching other systems.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Encryption at rest, layer by layer: disk, database, field
question: Why bind the row id and column name as associated data when encrypting a field?
options: It makes the ciphertext shorter
It hides the row id
Decryption fails if an encrypted value is moved to another row or column, so swaps are detected
It removes the need for a nonce
explain: Associated data is authenticated but not encrypted. Decrypting with different associated data raises InvalidTag, as the demo shows. It does not hide or shorten anything, and AES-GCM still needs a unique nonce per encryption.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: How DLP recognises sensitive content
question: What does exact data match add over a pattern-based SSN detector?
options: It finds SSNs in images
It encrypts the SSN before sending
It confirms the number is one of your own records (via salted hashes) and can check for matching fields from the same row nearby
It removes the need for a pattern
explain: EDM compares hashes of found values against hashes of your table, and then looks for secondary fields from the same record, which cuts false positives sharply. It still needs a pattern-based type to find the primary element first.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Disposal as a process: Morgan Stanley's drives and the certificate
question: A vendor returns a PDF titled 'Certificate of Destruction' listing a batch number but no serial numbers or method. What should the asset owner do?
options: Accept it: the title says destruction
File it and close the ticket
Reject it until it lists each device's serial number, the sanitisation method and technique, and who verified it, then reconcile against the inventory
Ask the vendor to add a company logo
explain: A certificate is only evidence if it can be matched device by device to the inventory and says what was done and by whom (SP 800-88 Rev. 2's list). In Morgan Stanley's case, documents that were not certificates of destruction at all went unreviewed.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Batch-dependent numerics and the token that flips
question: You must guarantee that one request gets the same tokens no matter what else is in the batch. Which property is the one you actually need?
options: Batch invariance: each output element's reduction order is fixed regardless of batch size and of the request's position in the batch.
Run-to-run determinism of every kernel.
A fixed random seed attached to each request.
Greedy decoding instead of sampling.
explain: Run-to-run determinism is already true of a typical forward pass and does not help, because the batch changes between runs. A seed fixes the sampler, not the logits. Greedy removes the RNG but makes the near-tie worse. Only batch invariance pins the arithmetic your request sees.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Inside the simulator: one thread, one seed, simulated time
question: A replica computes its election deadline as `time.time() + random_timeout()`, using Python's real clock, while everything else goes through the simulator. What breaks?
options: Nothing: the timeout value still comes from the seeded generator
Replay: the deadline now depends on wall-clock time, so the same seed can schedule different events
Only performance: real clock reads are slower than simulated ones
Safety of the protocol in production
explain: Wall-clock time differs between runs and is unrelated to simulated time, so the deadline, and every event that depends on it, changes from run to run. One leak like this destroys reproducibility for the whole simulation. All time must come from the simulated clock.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: DevSecOps: security checks on the path from commit to cloud
question: A company locks down its cloud console with MFA and short sessions, but its deploy pipeline holds a long-lived admin key. Where should an attacker aim?
options: At the console, because it holds the most permissions
At the pipeline: anyone who can make it run their code inherits its admin key without touching the console
At the developer's laptop only, since pipelines cannot be attacked
Nowhere: MFA on the console protects every path into the account
explain: Console MFA protects one door. The pipeline is another identity with the same or more power, and it acts on code it is given. Controlling its input or its runner is as good as owning its key.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: CircleCI 2023: when the platform holding your secrets is breached
question: CircleCI encrypted customer secrets at rest. Why were they still exposed?
options: The encryption algorithm was broken
The attacker extracted the encryption keys from a running process, which must hold them to use the secrets
Secrets were stored in plain text by mistake
The customers' own laptops were compromised
explain: The report says data was encrypted at rest but keys were extracted from a running process. At-rest encryption protects stolen disks and backups, not a service that is running and compromised.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Terraform state: the file that holds every secret
question: A team marks every secret variable `sensitive = true` and says their state is now safe to share with all engineers. What is wrong?
options: sensitive only redacts CLI and UI output; the values are still in the state file in plain text
Nothing: sensitive values are encrypted in state
sensitive deletes the values after apply
State files never contain variables
explain: The real run shows the password twice in terraform.tfstate. To keep a value out of state you need ephemeral values or write-only arguments, or a secret manager referenced at runtime.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Drift detection: when the cloud stops matching the code
question: A scheduled `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` on main returns 2. Nobody merged anything since the last apply. What does it most likely mean?
options: Terraform crashed
No changes are needed
Something changed outside Terraform: drift that the owners must review
The state file is encrypted
explain: Exit code 2 means the plan succeeded and has changes. With no new code, those changes come from the live side: drift. Exit code 1 would be an error.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: The forward process: masking as noise, and its exact reverse
question: In a reverse step from t to s, a masked position stays masked with probability s/t. What happens when s = 0?
options: Every masked position is revealed in this step
Nothing is revealed, because s/t = 0 means no change
Half of the masked positions are revealed
The visible tokens are remasked
explain: With s = 0 the probability of staying masked is 0/t = 0, so every remaining mask must be filled. The last step of any schedule ends at s = 0 and finishes the sequence.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Where diffusion LMs stand: results, block diffusion, and limits
question: A team needs exact KV caching and variable-length outputs but wants some parallel decoding. Which design fits best?
options: Pure masked diffusion over a fixed 1024-token canvas
BERT with a 15% masking ratio
An autoregressive model sampled at high temperature
Block diffusion with a small block size, autoregressive across blocks
explain: Block diffusion freezes finished blocks, so their keys and values are cached exactly and generation can continue block after block. Diffusion inside each block still commits several tokens per pass. A fixed canvas has neither property, and BERT cannot sample text.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Splitting the phases: pools, ratios and parallelism
question: Using DistServe's equations with D = 0.1 s and K = 1.6, which 2-GPU plan gives lower average TTFT at a low arrival rate of 2 req/s?
options: Intra-op (tensor): it cuts execution time to D/K, and queueing is small at low rate
Neither; one GPU is always better
Inter-op (pipeline): it doubles capacity
They are identical at low rate
explain: At R = 2 the intra-op TTFT is 0.0625 + 0.0045 = about 0.067 s, while inter-op is 0.1 + 0.0028 = about 0.103 s. Execution time dominates at low load, so cutting it wins. At high load the queueing term flips the order.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: What deleting a file really does: a FAT walk-through
question: A deleted FAT file's entry says first cluster 3, size 5,000 bytes, 1,024-byte clusters. Unknown to you, the file was stored in clusters 3, 4, 9, 10 and 11. You recover 5,000 bytes from cluster 3 onward. What do you get?
options: The exact file, because FAT keeps a backup chain
The first 2,048 bytes correct, then whatever sits in clusters 5 to 7
Nothing, because a deleted entry has no first cluster
The exact file, because FAT never fragments files
explain: Clusters 3 and 4 are right (2,048 bytes). Deletion zeroed the chain, so the jump to 9 is lost and you read clusters 5, 6, 7 instead. The entry keeps the first cluster; there is no backup chain; and FAT files can fragment.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Linux ext4: superblock, inodes, extents and the journal
question: An ext4 image has 128-byte inodes. A colleague asks for each file's creation time. What do you answer?
options: 128-byte inodes have no creation time field; use other sources (journal, logs, application data) for when files appeared
Read crtime at offset 0x90
Use ctime, which is the creation time
Use dtime, which records the first write
explain: crtime exists only in the larger inode format. ctime is the inode change time, not creation (the prereq's backdating trick relies on that difference), and dtime is deletion time.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Shortcuts, Jump Lists, ShellBags and the Recycle Bin
question: An LNK file in Recent says its target was written 2026-03-02 14:01:07. The LNK file itself was created 2026-03-04 09:12. What can you say?
options: The target was modified on 4 March
The LNK file is forged because its dates disagree
The target was deleted on 4 March
When the shortcut was last updated, the target's write time was 2 March 14:01:07; the user most likely first opened it through this account on 4 March
explain: Header times describe the target as it was when the link was last updated; the LNK's own creation time reflects when the shortcut was made. Different dates are normal, not a sign of forgery.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Anti-forensics from the defender's side: what each trick leaves
question: Which observation is the strongest sign of deliberate anti-forensics rather than normal use?
options: Files in the Recycle Bin
Last-access times that are hours old
A Security log containing event 1102 shortly after an unusual administrator logon
Large free space on the disk
explain: Event 1102 records that the audit log was cleared, which ordinary users do not do, and timing next to an unusual admin logon raises it further. Recycle Bin items, lazy access times and free space are normal.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Vamana: RobustPrune and the alpha knob
question: In the toy example, alpha = 1.2 kept the edge p to E even though B is closer to E than p is. Which statement explains why that edge is useful?
options: E is p's nearest neighbor
Going through B would bring a search only slightly closer to E (5.00 vs 5.39), so a direct edge gives much faster progress toward points near E
Vamana keeps every edge longer than 5
alpha only affects the build pass, not which edges exist
explain: Under alpha = 1.2 an edge is dropped only if the detour node is closer to the target by a factor of 1.2 (for E: within 5.39 / 1.2 = 4.49). B is at 5.00, only about 7 percent closer, so the hop through B makes little progress. Keeping long edges where detours are weak is what shrinks the number of hops.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
question: Why can DPO ignore the partition function $Z(x)$, which sums over every possible response?
options: It is always equal to 1 for a normalized language model
It depends only on the prompt, so it cancels in the reward difference that Bradley-Terry uses
DPO estimates it with Monte Carlo samples from the policy
It is absorbed into the learning rate
explain: $\beta \log Z(x)$ is the same for every answer to a given prompt. Bradley-Terry compares two answers to the same prompt through $r(y_w) - r(y_l)$, so the term cancels exactly. No sampling or approximation is needed.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: ORPO and SimPO: dropping the reference model
question: A team must align a 7B base model on one GPU with tight memory and has paired preference data but no SFT checkpoint yet. Which method fits best?
options: DPO, because it is the most widely used
KTO, because it needs no pairs
ORPO, because it trains from the base model in one stage with no reference model
IPO, because it regularizes better
explain: ORPO combines the SFT loss with the odds-ratio penalty, so it needs neither a prior SFT stage nor a reference copy of the model. DPO, IPO and KTO all assume a reference (normally an SFT model) is available.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Backfilling history without overwriting newer writes
question: In DBLog, why drop a chunk row whose key changed inside the window, rather than keep the chunk's value?
options: The chunk value is always older than the log event
The select's exact log position is unknown, so its value may be older than the event; the event is at least as new, so emitting it alone is always safe
Dropping rows makes chunks smaller and faster to emit
Log events contain more columns than chunk rows
explain: The select happened somewhere inside the window, so for a key changed in the window it may have read the value before or after that change. Keeping the log event, which is the latest committed change for that key up to that point, is correct either way; keeping the chunk row could reintroduce an older value.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Probes: kprobes, tracepoints, fentry, uprobes and profile
question: In a kretprobe on a function, you try to print arg0 to see which file descriptor was passed in. What goes wrong, and what fixes it?
options: Arguments are not available at return in a kretprobe; save them in a map keyed by tid at entry, or use fexit, which still has args
Nothing; arg0 is preserved for kretprobe
kretprobes cannot access any data at all; use printf instead
You must cast arg0 to a pointer first
explain: A kretprobe only has retval: argument registers may have been overwritten by the time the function returns. Save what you need at entry, keyed by tid, or use fexit, whose args remain available on return.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
question: A colleague's kprobe-based script worked last year but now fails to attach after a kernel upgrade. What is the most likely cause?
options: The verifier became stricter about printf
bpftrace no longer supports kprobes
Tracepoints replaced all kprobes
The probed kernel function was renamed, removed or changed, because kprobes target internal, unstable functions
explain: kprobes can attach to almost any kernel function, but those functions are not an API. Tracepoints, or fentry with BTF types, are more resilient. By default bpftrace exits with an error if any probe fails to attach, unless the missing_probes config is set to warn or ignore.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Per-channel scales, calibration, and quantization-aware training
question: Why do the gradients in QAT use the straight-through estimator instead of the true derivative of round()?
options: The true derivative is zero almost everywhere, so no gradient would reach the weights
round() is not implemented on GPUs
The estimator makes training faster but changes the final model format
It removes the need for calibration
explain: round() is a step function: its derivative is zero except at the jumps, where it is undefined. Treating the quantizer as identity inside the clipping range lets gradients flow so the float weights can move to positions that quantize well.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Pulse Secure and FortiOS, 2019: file reads that leaked passwords
question: In the toy server, why is '/assets/html5/../../../../data/sessions.db' served by the vulnerable check?
options: Python's normpath has a bug
The file is inside the web root
The rule tests the raw text for an allowed folder name, and only resolves the path after deciding
The '..' characters are removed automatically
explain: The decision is made on the text, which contains OPEN_DIR, so the '..' refusal is skipped. The fixed version decides on the resolved location, which is outside the root.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Exposure management: what you show the internet, continuously
question: Your external scan finds a NetScaler Gateway on an address that is not in the inventory. What should happen first?
options: Ignore it until a vulnerability scanner flags a CVE
Treat it as a finding now: find the owner, confirm the version and support status, and block it if no owner appears
Run an exploit against it to prove it is vulnerable
Delete it from the scan results
explain: An unowned internet-facing edge product is a risk before any CVE is known: nobody patches it or reads its logs. Testing it with an exploit is out of bounds unless you own it and have authorisation; ownership comes first.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Responding to a compromised appliance: evidence, rebuild, rotate
question: A Cisco firewall's core dump analysis returns 'Compromise Detected'. Under ED 25-03, what should you do with the device first?
options: Disconnect it from the network but keep it powered on, report it and work on eviction
Reboot it to clear the malware
Install the patch and put it back in service
Power it off immediately
explain: Disconnecting stops the intruder using it; keeping power preserves memory for analysis. A reboot does not remove this malware (the directive later required a full power removal as part of remediation, after evidence collection).

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Length penalties inside RL: Kimi k1.5 and DAPO
question: In a GRPO group, all 8 sampled responses are correct but their lengths differ. With correctness reward only, what is the policy gradient signal from this group?
options: Zero: every reward is equal, so every advantage is 0, and length gets no push either way
Strongly favors the shortest response
Strongly favors the longest response
Negative for all responses, since the mean is subtracted
explain: Equal rewards give zero advantages, so the group teaches nothing. Kimi's length reward breaks the tie inside such groups, which is exactly where length can be cut without hurting accuracy.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Where a sensor sits: kernel callbacks, minifilters and network filters
question: Why does an antimalware vendor bother to ship an ELAM driver?
options: To make the sensor's network traffic faster
Because Windows refuses to load any driver without ELAM
To let users uninstall the product without admin rights
To start before other boot drivers and to qualify its service to run as a protected (PPL) antimalware process
explain: ELAM drivers initialize before other boot-start drivers and can decide whether those load. The ELAM driver also carries the certificate information Windows uses to let the vendor's service run as a protected antimalware service, shielding it from tampering by ordinary admin processes.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Process injection as telemetry: Sysmon events 8, 10 and 25
question: Sysmon event 10 shows `C:\Users\Public\upd.exe` opening lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1010. What did the program get?
options: Permission to terminate LSASS
Only the process name
Query-limited information plus the right to read LSASS memory, enough to copy credentials out of it
The right to start a thread inside LSASS
explain: 0x1010 is PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION (0x1000) plus PROCESS_VM_READ (0x0010). Reading LSASS memory is how credential dumping works; an unsigned program in a public folder asking for it is a strong signal.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Attack surface reduction rules: blocking risky behaviours
question: You enable 'Block all Office applications from creating child processes' in Audit mode. Over a week, which event shows how often it would have fired?
explain: 1122 is the audit-mode event (Microsoft lists 1122, 1125, 1132 and 1134 for audit detections); 1121 is a rule firing in block mode. 5007 is a Defender configuration change.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: What kernel sensors cost: CrowdStrike Channel File 291 (July 2024)
question: Why did earlier IPC Template Instances work in production, although the 20 vs 21 mismatch existed since February?
options: They were never deployed
They ran only on Linux
They used a wildcard for the 21st criterion, which the interpreter skips without reading the missing input
Windows patched the bug in March
explain: The RCA explains that wildcard matching for the 21st input meant the out-of-bounds value was never read. The first instance with a non-wildcard 21st criterion triggered the read.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Combinatorial optimisation and factorial HMMs
question: Why does the one-change-per-step constraint in AFAMAP make sense for energy data?
options: Appliances are physically prevented from switching together
It forces the kettle to be modelled separately
It removes the need for training data
It restates the switch continuity principle: at short sample intervals, simultaneous switching is rare, and the constraint shrinks the search enormously
explain: Simultaneous switches are possible (our minute 45), but rare at short sampling intervals. Assuming at most one change per step turns an exponential joint search into one over N single-chain changes, which is what makes the convex relaxation efficient. It is a modelling assumption, so it will occasionally be wrong.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Cleaning: Unicode, case, punctuation and legal suffixes
question: Profiles are cleaned with NFKC, casefold and suffix stripping before indexing. The query parser lowercases the recruiter's text but does nothing else. A recruiter searches `Brightline Labs, Inc.`. What happens?
options: It matches, because lowercasing is enough
It misses: the query key is `brightline labs, inc.` while the indexed key is `brightline labs`
It matches only r3, which was typed the same way
explain: The index stores cleaned keys, so a raw query string with a comma and suffix never equals them. The fix is to run the exact same normalizer on the query side.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: A tenant: the cloud directory behind every Microsoft 365 login
question: An attacker has Ravi's Exchange Online access token. Which claim tells a defender which application obtained it?
options: `azp` (or `appid` in v1.0 tokens), the client application ID
`tid`, because it names the tenant
`aud`, because it names the application
`amr`, because it records the app's sign-in method
explain: `azp` (v2.0) or `appid` (v1.0) identify the client using the token. `aud` names the resource the token is for (Exchange Online here), `tid` the tenant and `amr` how the user authenticated. Investigations use `azp` or `appid` to spot an unexpected client.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Case: Midnight Blizzard inside Microsoft's own tenant (2024)
question: Why did Conditional Access requiring MFA for corporate users not stop the mailbox reads, even if it had been configured in the corporate tenant?
options: Because the reads were done by apps with an application permission, and user-scoped Conditional Access does not apply to service principals
Because EWS does not support tokens
Because residential proxies bypass all policy
Because full_access_as_app disables Conditional Access tenant-wide
explain: App-only tokens are issued to the service principal through the client credentials grant; there is no user sign-in for a user policy to evaluate. Microsoft documents that user-scoped policies do not block service principals.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Token theft and replay, and binding tokens to devices
question: A user with a FIDO2 passkey has an infostealer on a personal laptop that copies the browser's Entra session cookie. Which control would stop the attacker reusing it from their own computer?
options: A Conditional Access policy requiring a compliant device (or Token Protection where supported), so the attacker's machine fails the device check
Requiring a stronger passkey
Shorter passwords
Blocking device code flow
explain: The passkey already did its job at sign-in; the theft happened after. Only a control evaluated at token use, such as a device compliance requirement or device-bound tokens, rejects the replay from another machine.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: The logs: sign-ins, audit, Graph activity and MailItemsAccessed
question: An investigator on Entra ID P1 learns of a compromise that began 45 days ago. No diagnostic settings were configured. What sign-in data is available for the first two weeks of the intrusion?
options: None: P1 keeps sign-in and audit logs for 30 days, and data not exported before it aged out cannot be recovered
All of it: sign-in logs are kept for 90 days
Only interactive sign-ins
All of it, after upgrading to P2
explain: Microsoft's retention table gives 30 days for P1 and P2. Upgrades are not retroactive, and expired data is gone unless it was archived. This is why exporting logs is a day-one task.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Inside epoll: interest list, ready list, epoll_wait
question: A loop calls epoll_wait(ep, evs, 64, -1). 200 sockets are ready. What happens to the 136 that do not fit?
options: They are dropped and will not be reported again until new data arrives
They stay ready; later epoll_wait calls round-robin through them
epoll_wait fails with EINVAL because maxevents is too small
The kernel grows the evs array to 200 entries
explain: maxevents only limits how many entries one call copies out. The epoll_wait(2) notes say successive calls round-robin through the ready set, precisely so a few busy descriptors cannot starve the rest.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: The winner's curse: why the best public score is too high
question: In the toy, what happens to the expected inflation of the best-of-100 winner if you keep N = 100 but grow the public set from 50 to 200 queries?
options: It roughly halves, because the noise in each system's mean scales like 1/sqrt(n)
It drops to about a quarter, because inflation scales like 1/n
It stays the same, because the number of systems is unchanged
It grows, because more queries give more chances to get lucky
explain: Each system's mean has noise of about s/sqrt(n). Four times as many queries halves that standard deviation, and the expected maximum of 100 draws halves with it. Selection bias shrinks with more queries but never vanishes while you keep selecting.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: From bug to control: why exploit mitigations exist
question: A team ships a C parser with canaries, NX and ASLR all enabled. A fuzzer finds a heap overflow in it. What is the right response?
options: Fix it as a security bug: mitigations raise exploit cost but do not remove the bug, and the overflow may combine with other bugs
Fix it with normal priority: the mitigations make it unexploitable
Leave it: heap bugs cannot reach the return address, so canaries make it harmless
Disable ASLR during debugging so the crash is reproducible, then close it
explain: Mitigations make exploitation harder, not impossible. Heap overflows in particular are not touched by stack canaries at all, and an overflow can corrupt function pointers or be paired with an information leak. Treat it as a vulnerability and patch it.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Why one leaked pointer defeats ASLR, and guessing at scale
question: A server forks a new worker for each connection from one long-running parent, and never calls exec. An attacker can crash workers at will. Which property makes guessing much easier than the entropy suggests?
options: Forked workers get a new layout each time, so failures are independent
Every forked worker inherits the parent's layout and canary, so information learned from one attempt still holds in the next
fork disables NX
fork leaks the canary to the network
explain: fork copies the parent's address space, including the randomized layout and the canary. Knowledge accumulates across crashes, which is the brute-force case in the PaX documentation and the precondition for Blind ROP. Re-exec on restart restores independence.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Memory tagging and hardened allocators against heap bugs
question: Why did Apple's MIE insist on synchronous tag checking for key attack surfaces?
options: Synchronous mode uses fewer tag bits
Asynchronous mode only works on Android
Synchronous mode disables ASLR
Asynchronous mode reports the fault after the access, leaving a window in which corrupted memory may already be used
explain: In asynchronous mode the mismatching access completes and the fault is delivered later. Apple's post argues that this race window is unacceptable against attackers, so MIE uses synchronous checks, always on.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: What each mitigation does not stop, and where to practise
question: An exploit for a 64-bit service first uses an out-of-bounds read to print a pointer into libc, then overflows a stack buffer. Which mitigation does the first step most directly cancel?
options: NX
Full RELRO
MTE in synchronous mode
ASLR, because one leaked libc pointer reveals libc's slide and every libc address
explain: Randomization hides addresses only while the slide is secret. A single leaked pointer into libc reveals the slide, so all of libc's code is again at known addresses. This is why leaks are treated as serious bugs in their own right.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Fixing it: pad, align, or stop sharing writes
question: Spot the bug: `struct Stats { std::atomic<long> hits; std::atomic<long> misses; };` with `alignas(64) Stats per_thread[8];`. Each thread writes only its own element. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: the array is aligned, so elements are on separate lines
Each element is only 16 bytes, so four threads' elements share each 64-byte line
alignas cannot be used on arrays
The two atomics in one element will falsely share
explain: alignas on the array aligns only its start. Each element is 16 bytes, so elements 0 to 3 share the first line and 4 to 7 the second. Put alignas on the struct type (so sizeof becomes 64) instead. Fields inside one element are written by the same thread, so they do not cause false sharing.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Buying rounds with local work, and when that stops working
question: In the original experiments, which result shows that more local computation is not always better?
options: On the IID MNIST split, E = 20 with B = 10 needed 18 rounds instead of 626
The model reached a higher final accuracy (99.44 percent) than the gradient-averaging baseline
A client fraction of C = 0.1 worked about as well as C = 1.0
On the non-IID split, E = 5 with full local batches needed 1000 rounds while single gradients needed 483
explain: That row is the one setting in the table slower than the FedSGD baseline, a 0.5x speedup. It is the fingerprint of local work pulling clients apart. The Shakespeare LSTM shows the same effect more dramatically: with very large E, training can plateau or diverge.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-gamma: expand every neighbor list by gamma
question: An index is built with M = 32 and gamma = 12. A query arrives with predicate selectivity s = 0.25. Roughly how many neighbors will the search compute distances for at a typical visited node?
options: 384, the whole stored list
96, all passing neighbors
At most 32: the passing neighbors are truncated to M
explain: About 384 x 0.25 = 96 neighbors pass, but ACORN truncates the filtered list to the first M = 32 before computing distances. The predicate is evaluated on up to 384 entries (cheap), distances on at most 32 (expensive). 8 would be plain HNSW's expectation.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Fine-grained experts: split each expert into m slices
question: Why is the combinatorial count, not the expert count, the quantity the paper highlights?
options: Because more combinations means more FLOPs
Because routers need at least a billion options to converge
Because GPUs schedule experts by combination
Because each token's computation is a sum over its chosen experts, so more possible subsets means a more precisely targeted mix of knowledge at the same cost
explain: A token's MoE output is the gated sum of its chosen experts. With 120 possible pairs, many different kinds of tokens must share the same pair. With billions of possible 8-subsets of small experts, the token can assemble a closer fit. FLOPs are identical in both designs.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Putting it together: routing in DeepSeek-V3
question: DeepSeek-V3 relies on the bias method yet still keeps a sequence-wise balance loss with alpha = 0.0001. What is the best justification?
options: The bias method does not work without an auxiliary loss
The bias balances load across whole batches; the tiny loss only guards against extreme imbalance within a single sequence, while staying too weak to cause meaningful interference gradients
The loss replaces the bias during the final 500B tokens
It is needed to train the router weights at all
explain: The report calls it complementary: the main balancing is aux-loss-free, and the sequence-wise term exists just to avoid extreme per-sequence imbalance. Its alpha is ten times smaller than the 0.001 baseline used in the loss-free paper. Router weights are trained by the language-modeling loss through the gate values.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-3: producer and consumer warps, then ping-pong
question: A teammate proposes giving the producer warpgroup as many registers as the consumers, "to be fair." What is the most likely effect?
options: Faster loads, because TMA needs registers for each byte copied
No effect, because register counts are fixed per kernel
Fewer registers for the consumers, forcing smaller tiles or spills in the math path
Better ping-pong, because both warpgroups can then do softmax
explain: TMA is issued by a single thread and copies data without staging it in registers. Registers given to the producer are taken from the consumers, which hold the accumulators; the paper deallocates producer registers and reallocates them to consumers for exactly this reason.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Why LLM serving needs its own attention engine
question: Which of these does FlashInfer treat as run-time input to its scheduler rather than as a compile-time kernel parameter?
options: The head dimension
Whether logits are soft-capped
The KV length of each request in this step
The data type of the KV cache
explain: Head dimension, the variant (such as soft-capping) and dtypes are fixed when the kernel is JIT compiled. Per-request lengths change every step, so they go to the plan function, which produces a fresh work assignment without recompiling.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Tile sizes, GQA head fusion and JIT attention variants
question: You want attention with RoPE applied inside the kernel (instead of a separate RoPE pass that writes rotated Q and K to HBM). Which variant hooks do you implement?
options: LogitsMask
OutputTransform
QueryTransform and KeyTransform
ValueTransform only
explain: RoPE rotates query and key vectors before their dot product, which is exactly what the query and key transform functors are for. The paper uses them for fused RoPE in StreamingLLM. A mask or output hook acts too late, and values are not rotated.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Relation to diffusion, and rectified flow in Stable Diffusion 3
question: Why does SD3 sample training timesteps from a logit-normal instead of uniformly?
options: The velocity regression is easiest near t = 0 and t = 1, so spending more training samples on intermediate t gives a better model
Uniform sampling makes the ODE solver unstable at test time
Logit-normal sampling removes the need for classifier-free guidance
It makes the paths straight without reflow
explain: Esser et al. argue that near the ends the target is easy to predict (close to pure data or pure noise), and confirm experimentally that rf/lognorm(0.00, 1.00) beats uniform rectified flow. It reweights the loss over time; it does not change the paths or the sampler.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Model checking a consensus core: votes, quorums and restarts
question: Which configuration makes TLC report a OneValue violation even with AllowRestart = FALSE?
options: 3 acceptors, quorum size 2
5 acceptors, quorum size 3
5 acceptors, quorum size 4
4 acceptors, quorum size 2
explain: Two quorums can be disjoint when 2 x QSize <= number of acceptors. With 4 acceptors and size 2, {a1, a2} and {a3, a4} share no one, so each can choose a different value. TLC's trace is 4 votes long.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Verus: proving Rust functions with requires, ensures and invariants
question: Which statement about Verus ghost code is true?
options: Spec functions can use u32 overflow semantics to match the code
Proof functions run at startup to check the lemmas
Spec and proof code are erased before compilation, so they add no run-time cost
Exec code may call spec functions to compute values at run time
explain: Ghost code exists only for verification. Spec functions use mathematical int and nat, proof functions are checked statically, and exec code cannot call either to compute run-time values.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Scaling factors: sliding a tensor into FP8's window
question: With delayed scaling, the scale for step t comes from amaxes recorded up to step t-1. A layer's activations suddenly grow 4x at step t. What happens at step t?
options: Training stops with a NaN because E4M3 has no infinity
The largest values exceed 448 after scaling and saturate to 448, so they are clipped for that step
TE detects the overflow and skips the optimizer step
Nothing: the scale is recomputed from step t before casting
explain: Delayed scaling reacts one step late. At step t the old scale pushes the large values past 448 and they saturate (clip). The new amax enters the history, so step t+1 uses a smaller scale. Current scaling avoids this lag at the cost of an extra pass over the tensor.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: When low precision fails: outliers, SwiGLU and debugging a run
question: Setting LLaMA2-7B's four massive activations to their mean values leaves the model working, while setting them to zero collapses it. What does that imply for quantization?
options: They are noise and can be clipped to the format maximum
They only matter at inference, not in training
They should be removed with weight decay
They are essential fixed biases: a quantizer must represent them, and must not let them flush their neighbours to zero
explain: Sun et al. conclude they work like constant bias terms. Clipping or zeroing them changes the model's function, and a shared scale sized for them can zero ordinary values: that is why per-block scaling, Smooth-SwiGLU style per-channel scales and higher-precision layers exist.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
question: Spot the bug. A program writes `state.tmp`, calls `rename("state.tmp", "state")`, then fsyncs the directory. It never fsyncs `state.tmp`. What can a crash leave behind?
options: Nothing bad: the directory fsync also flushes every file in it
Two files named state
A durable name `state` that points to a file whose new data never reached disk, so it may be empty or partial
The old `state` file, always, because rename is atomic
explain: The directory fsync makes the rename durable, but it does not flush the data of the files it names. Without an fsync of the temporary file before the rename, the name can survive while the contents do not. Atomic rename only protects what other processes see while the system is running.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: What vulnerability research is, and the rules you work under
question: You find a crash by fuzzing a library on your laptop, then notice a company runs the same library on its public API. What is the right next step?
options: Report the bug to the library's maintainers privately, with your local reproducer
Send the crashing input to the company's API to confirm it is affected
Publish the reproducer immediately so users can protect themselves
Ask the company for a reward before telling them anything
explain: Your local reproduction is already proof. Hitting the company's API is testing a system you have no permission to test, publishing first leaves every user exposed, and demanding payment as a condition of reporting can be extortion. The maintainers can fix it for everyone, including that company.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing good harnesses: fast, deterministic and structure-aware
question: Your harness calls a function that writes a log line and appends to a global cache on every call. What two problems does this cause?
options: Logging slows every run, and the global cache makes later runs depend on earlier inputs, so crashes may not reproduce
None, as long as the program does not crash
libFuzzer refuses to compile code with globals
The global cache is counted as new coverage, which is good
explain: The libFuzzer docs ask for fast targets without logging and without global state. A cache carried between runs means a crash can depend on a sequence of inputs, and the saved single input will not reproduce it.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Measuring fuzzers honestly: coverage, crashes and statistics
question: Why did Klees et al. recommend the Mann Whitney U test rather than comparing average crash counts?
options: Fuzzing results vary widely between runs and are not normally distributed, so a non-parametric test tells whether a difference is likely real
It runs faster than computing an average
It counts unique bugs automatically
Averages cannot be computed for crash counts
explain: Run-to-run variance is large and skewed. Averages can differ by chance; the test estimates whether one configuration's results tend to exceed the other's, without assuming a bell curve.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Symbolic and concolic execution: solving for the input
question: A fuzzer stalls at the check `if (crc32(data) == header->crc)`. Why might symbolic execution also struggle here, while a FUZZING_BUILD_MODE build would not?
options: Solving for data that hashes to a given CRC through symbolic expressions of a whole loop is expensive, while the fuzzing build simply skips the check
Symbolic execution cannot handle any checksums
Fuzzing builds compute CRCs faster
SMT solvers do not support integers
explain: CRC32 is linear and solvable in principle, but expressed symbolically over a long buffer it is a heavy constraint. Disabling the check in a fuzzing-only build is far cheaper. For true cryptographic hashes, solving is infeasible.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Why exact matching fails and what an edit distance counts
question: A search box accepts any dictionary word within 2 Levenshtein edits of the query. For which query is this rule most likely to return junk?
options: `cat` (3 letters)
`restaurant` (10 letters)
`levenshtein` (11 letters)
All three are equally safe because the threshold is the same
explain: Two edits can rewrite 2 of the 3 letters of `cat`, so `cut`, `bag`, `act` and many other 3-letter words all match. For a 10 or 11 letter word, 2 edits keep most of the string intact. This is why search engines scale the allowed edits with term length (lesson 6).

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Indexes that skip most strings: trigram filters and BK-trees
question: In a BK-tree, the query is at distance 3 from a node and the search radius is 1. Which child subtrees are searched?
options: Only the child labelled 3
Children labelled 2, 3 and 4
Children labelled 0 to 4
All children, because 3 > 1
explain: Any match $u$ in a child labelled $i$ has $d(u,\text{node}) = i$ and $d(q,u) \le 1$, so by the triangle inequality $|i-3| \le 1$, giving $i \in \{2,3,4\}$. Every other child provably contains no match.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
question: A quad's code is (0.30, 0.40, 0.90, 0.20). What is the code of the same four stars if the labels A and B had been swapped?
explain: Swapping A and B turns the frame 180 degrees about (0.5, 0.5), so every coordinate becomes 1 minus itself. Here the original has xC + xD = 1.2, which is more than 1, and the swapped one 0.8, so the canonical labeling is the swapped one (then C and D trade places to get xC <= xD).

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: From an accepted match to a WCS header, and the triangle alternative
question: Groth's triangle matcher discards matched triangle pairs whose log perimeter ratio is far from the average. Why does that remove false matches?
options: False matches have larger perimeters
All true matches share one magnification between the lists, so their log perimeter ratios cluster, while false matches scatter
The perimeter is not scale invariant
It removes triangles with clockwise orientation
explain: Between two lists there is a single scale factor. Every truly corresponding triangle shows the same perimeter ratio; coincidental shape matches come from unrelated triangles of any size, so their ratios spread out. The same idea appears in Astrometry.net's scale-range check.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Better cells on the sphere: S2 cubes and H3 hexagons
question: How many cells does H3 resolution 2 have in total?
explain: c(r) = 2 + 120 x 7^r, so c(2) = 2 + 120 x 49 = 5,882. 122 is resolution 0 and 842 is resolution 1. The 12 pentagons are included in the count.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Warp and affine: an inverse map plus a border rule
question: A 5-tap filter on the row 10, 40, 90, 160 needs index -1 while computing output 0. Which rule returns 40 there?
options: REPLICATE
WRAP
REFLECT
REFLECT101
explain: REFLECT101 mirrors without repeating the edge, so index -1 maps to index 1, whose value is 40. REPLICATE clamps to index 0 and gives 10, REFLECT repeats the edge so it also gives 10, and WRAP folds to index 3, or 160. Only REFLECT101 reaches past the edge pixel to a real neighbour.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
question: You call torch.cuda.empty_cache() while a 3 MiB tensor is alive in a 20 MiB segment. How much of that segment is returned to the driver?
options: All 20 MiB, because only 3 MiB is in use
17 MiB, the free part
None of it, because the segment is split around a live block
3 MiB, the live tensor is moved to the small pool
explain: The allocator can only cudaFree a whole segment, and only when no block in it is in use. A partly used segment keeps all of its memory reserved, including the free 17 MiB.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Fixed-size suballocation for the KV cache, and diagnosing OOMs
question: A training job OOMs. memory_allocated is 30 GB, memory_reserved is 39 GB on a 40 GB GPU, and memory_summary shows 8 GB of inactive split blocks. What should you try first?
options: Enable expandable_segments to avoid stranded slivers in fixed segments
Call empty_cache() before every step
Switch to a smaller block size for the KV cache
Lower garbage_collection_threshold to 0.1
explain: 8 GB free inside split segments is fragmentation, which empty_cache cannot release because those segments hold live tensors. Expandable segments target exactly that; max_split_size_mb is the documented fallback.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Shared memory banks and bank conflicts
question: All 32 threads of a warp read `s[7]` from a shared float array. How many passes does the access need?
options: 32, because every thread uses bank 7
16, because pairs of threads share a pass
1, because the word is broadcast
2, because reads of one bank are paired
explain: A bank conflict needs different addresses in the same bank. Here every thread asks for the same word, which the hardware broadcasts in a single pass.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: The SOL gap: ranking many kernels by what they can return
question: After rewriting a kernel it runs in 0.62 ms instead of 0.90 ms, but its Memory Throughput row fell from 48 percent to 41 percent. What do you conclude?
options: The rewrite is a regression: the kernel now uses the memory system less efficiently
The measurement must be wrong, since less time with the same work implies a higher percent of peak
The rewrite is a 1.45x win; a SOL row can fall when the work itself shrinks, and duration is the thing you validate against
Nothing can be concluded without re-running with cache control disabled
explain: If the rewrite removed traffic, for example by fusing a pass or improving reuse, the kernel moves fewer bytes in less time, and the percent of peak can fall while the duration improves. The triage guide says to validate every change against absolute kernel duration for exactly this reason. The percentages are for classification, not scoring.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Warps and SIMT: 32 threads, one instruction, and divergence
question: A block of 256 threads executes `if (threadIdx.x < 96) heavy(); else light();`. How many of its 8 warps diverge on this branch?
options: 0: 96 is a multiple of 32, so the split falls on a warp boundary
3: warps 0 to 2 run heavy()
8: any if statement makes every warp run both paths
1: only the warp containing thread 96
explain: Threads 0 to 95 are exactly warps 0, 1 and 2; threads 96 to 255 are warps 3 to 7. Every warp's 32 threads agree, so no warp has to run both paths. Divergence is a per-warp property, not a per-block one.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
question: Why does increasing k (retrieving more chunks) not solve global questions on a 1-million-token corpus?
options: Because embeddings cannot represent questions
Because LLMs cannot read more than 10 chunks
Because chunks overlap by 100 tokens
Because the retrieved set is still ranked by similarity to the question and bounded by the context window, so it is a biased sample, not the whole corpus
explain: Retrieval chooses what is similar to the question words, and the context window caps how much fits. For "main themes" the relevant evidence is everywhere, so any top-k set is a sample presented as if it were a global view.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: What GraphRAG costs and how its gains were measured
question: Your corpus doubles from 1M to 2M tokens with the same settings. Roughly what happens to extraction LLM calls?
options: They stay the same because the graph is reused
They roughly double, because extraction runs once per chunk
They grow quadratically with the number of entity pairs
They halve because chunks get larger
explain: Extraction is one prompt (plus gleaning) per chunk, so it scales linearly with the number of chunks. Summaries and reports depend on graph size, which also tends to grow.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Group-relative advantages: the baseline from sibling answers
question: A group of 4 answers gets rewards 1, 0, 1, 0. Using the population std, what is the advantage of each correct answer?
explain: Mean 0.5, population std 0.5, so (1 - 0.5) / 0.5 = +1.0. Wrong answers get -1.0.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Failure modes and fixes: dead groups, entropy collapse, length bias
question: Under the original GRPO normalization, two wrong answers have the same advantage -1, one with 100 tokens and one with 1,000. How does the per-token push-down compare?
options: Equal per token
The 1,000-token answer's tokens are pushed down 10 times more each
Wrong answers get no gradient in GRPO
The 1,000-token answer's tokens are pushed down 10 times less each
explain: Each output's token terms are divided by its length, so each token of the long answer gets one tenth of the weight. Long wrong answers are cheap, which can drive response length up. Token-level (DAPO) or constant (Dr. GRPO) normalization removes this.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: GTFS Realtime messages and decoding them in Python
question: A consumer receives FULL_DATASET feeds every 30 s. At 08:10 the feed has a TripUpdate for T1. At 08:10:30 it does not. What should the app show for T1?
options: No realtime information: fall back to the schedule and say so, or hide the prediction
Keep the 08:10 prediction until a new one arrives
Mark T1 as canceled
Assume T1 is now exactly on time
explain: Each FULL_DATASET message is the whole state. A dropped entity means there is no realtime information for it now. It is not a cancellation (that is an explicit CANCELED), and the reference warns that absence must not be read as on time.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Why a flame graph shows where time goes but not why
question: After a change, a service's IPC rises from 0.8 to 1.6, but requests take exactly as long as before. What is the most plausible explanation?
options: The counters are broken, since higher IPC always means faster code
The CPU clock frequency doubled
IPC is measured per core, so it cannot change per request
Cycles per request stayed the same while instructions per request doubled, for example from spinning or extra work
explain: IPC is a ratio. If time and cycles are unchanged, doubling IPC means twice as many instructions were retired per request: busy-waiting or redundant work. That is why IPC must be read alongside the raw instruction count.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Reading the numbers: generic events, pitfalls and top-down
question: On a cloud VM, `perf stat` prints `<not supported>` for cycles and instructions but shows task-clock and page-faults. Why?
options: The hypervisor does not expose the hardware PMU to this guest, so only software events work
perf is too old to know these events
The program ran too briefly to count any cycles
Those events need the :u modifier
explain: task-clock and page-faults are software events maintained by the kernel. Hardware events need PMU access, which a guest only gets if the hypervisor virtualizes it.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Branchless selection and secret-independent memory access
question: You compile the mask-based ct_select and find a conditional branch in the assembly. What is the right conclusion?
options: The source is wrong; masks always compile to branches
The compiler is free to do this because C does not promise timing; use a vetted primitive or a compiler barrier and re-check
Branches are fine as long as the branch predictor is accurate
Switch to -O0, which guarantees constant time
explain: C's semantics cover results, not timing, so optimisers may reintroduce branches. Libraries use techniques such as value barriers, and you verify the output. -O0 gives no such guarantee either.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Meltdown: reading kernel memory, and why KPTI fixes it
question: Which workload should you expect to slow down most after enabling KPTI on an older CPU without PCID?
options: A numerical simulation that rarely calls the kernel
A small-message server doing many system calls per request
A GPU training job
A program that only reads from its own heap
explain: The cost is paid on every kernel entry and exit (CR3 switches and TLB flushes without PCID). System-call-heavy code pays most, as the roughly 50 percent microbenchmark slowdown shows.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Trusted hardware: TPMs, measured boot and secure enclaves
question: BitLocker seals the disk key to PCR values. An attacker replaces the bootloader with one that logs keystrokes. What happens at the next boot?
options: The TPM detects the new bootloader's signature and deletes the key
Nothing: PCRs only record the kernel
The bootloader's hash changes the PCR value, so the TPM refuses to unseal the key and recovery is needed
The attacker's bootloader can reset the PCR to the old value
explain: Extend is one-way and order-sensitive, and the first 16 PCRs reset only with the TPM. A different bootloader produces different PCRs, so the sealed key stays locked.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: hugetlbfs: a reserved pool you map on purpose
question: A pool has 10 free pages and no reservations. Process A maps 8 huge pages with MAP_HUGETLB and touches 2 of them. Process B then tries to mmap 4 huge pages with MAP_HUGETLB. What happens?
options: B's mmap succeeds because HugePages_Free is 8
B's mmap succeeds, but B gets SIGBUS when it touches its third page
B's mmap fails with ENOMEM: Free is 8 but 6 are reserved for A, leaving 2
The kernel reclaims A's untouched reserved pages and gives them to B
explain: After A: Free = 10 - 2 = 8 and Rsvd = 8 - 2 = 6. Only Free - Rsvd = 2 pages are available, so B's 4-page reservation fails at mmap time. Reservations are not stolen back, and failing in mmap rather than at fault time is the whole point of reserving.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not
question: Which task is least likely to separate a pure SSM from a Transformer of the same size and data?
options: Recalling a phone number listed 3,000 tokens earlier
Copying a long string from the prompt
Zero-shot commonsense multiple choice such as PIQA or HellaSwag
Few-shot classification that must reuse exact label strings
explain: PIQA asks which of two solutions achieves an everyday physical goal; HellaSwag asks for the most plausible ending of a described situation. On such zero-shot commonsense tasks Mamba and Mamba-2 matched or beat the Transformer in the NVIDIA 8B study. The other three all need exact retrieval or copying from the context, which is where fixed-state models fall behind.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Serving a hybrid: prefix caching, rollback and chunked prefill
question: A server snapshots SSM states only at branch points found by Marconi-style speculative insertion, plus after each request's last decoded token. A new system prompt appears in requests 1, 2 and 3, each with a different question. Which is the first request whose Mamba layers can reuse the prompt?
options: Request 1
Request 2
Request 3
None of them, since recurrent states cannot be shared
explain: Request 1 creates the tree entry; nothing is shared yet. Request 2's insertion splits that edge at the end of the shared prompt, so its prefill saves the states there. Request 3 is the first to hit them. The paper accepts missing the second occurrence because hot prefixes are shared by many requests.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Local, shared and parallel attention, and converting a Transformer
question: You convert a 32-layer Transformer with 128 KiB of KV per token into a hybrid that keeps 1 attention layer in 8. How much KV per token remains?
options: 16 KiB
32 KiB
4 KiB
64 KiB
explain: KV is per attention layer: 128 KiB / 32 layers = 4 KiB per layer, and 4 layers remain, so 16 KiB, an 8x saving at long context. The Mamba layers add a fixed state that does not grow with context.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Why a raw query is a poor probe for an unsupervised encoder
question: A team has a new internal wiki, no click logs and no labeled queries. Which statement about their options is accurate?
options: A supervised dense retriever cannot be trained on in-domain labels yet, which is exactly the setting HyDE targets
They must label at least MS MARCO scale data before any dense retrieval works
BM25 is guaranteed to beat every dense method here
Contriever alone will match a fine-tuned retriever
explain: No relevance labels is the zero-shot setting of the HyDE paper. Contriever alone is usable but weak; BM25 is a strong baseline but not guaranteed best. The paper's answer is to move relevance modeling into a generative LLM.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Latency, cost, and when HyDE hurts
question: Your stack already uses a strong cross-encoder reranker that scores 72 nDCG@10 on your eval. A teammate wants to add generated passages to the reranker's query. Based on Weller et al., what should you expect and do?
options: A guaranteed gain, as on DPR
Likely no gain or a loss; measure on your own eval before shipping, and consider expansions only for the first stage or for shifted domains
No effect either way
A gain only if N is at least 8
explain: Weller et al. found strong models are generally harmed: MonoT5-3B lost 4.0 on DL19 and 14.7 on FiQA. Expansion tends to help weaker models or large format shifts, so it must be evaluated, not assumed.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: The Purdue model: levels from field devices to the enterprise
question: Why does NIST say outbound rules from the control network should be as strict as inbound ones?
options: Because outbound traffic is always faster
Because PLCs send too many emails
Because an infected control-network machine that can reach the internet or enterprise freely gives attackers a channel out and a path back in
Because inbound rules do not work in OT
explain: Malware on a Level 2 or 3 host needs to talk to its operator. Strict egress filtering blocks that and limits what a compromised host can reach. NIST calls unmanaged outbound connections 'a significant risk'.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Stuxnet, the controller that lied
question: An engineer uploads the PLC program through the plant's engineering workstation and it matches the approved version exactly. Why might that not be enough after a Stuxnet-style infection?
options: The workstation's PLC communication library may be intercepted, so the tool shows a cleaned view while the PLC runs extra code
Uploads are always encrypted
PLCs cannot store more than one program
Hashes cannot be computed for PLC code
explain: Stuxnet's fake s7otbxdx.dll hid its blocks from Step 7 reads. Verification must use a trusted path: a clean machine, vendor integrity features, or physical inspection of behaviour.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Segmentation, DMZs, one-way gateways and allowlisting
question: A plant wants dashboards in the head office showing live tank levels, and wants no possible inbound path. Which design fits?
options: A unidirectional gateway pushing historian data to a replica in the DMZ, read by the head office
A firewall rule allowing the head office to query the PLCs
A VPN from head office into the control zone
Putting the PLCs on the internet behind a password
explain: A data diode is physically one-way, so the replica can be fed without any route back into OT. Firewalls and VPNs can be misconfigured to allow inbound traffic; a diode cannot.
