lessonTitle: GitHub Actions attacks: pwn requests, injection and moving tags
question: A workflow uses `on: pull_request_target` and checks out the PR's head commit, but passes no secrets to any step. Is it safe?
options: No, but only for private repositories
Yes, because no secrets are referenced
Yes, if the job only runs npm install
No: the job still has a repository token with write access that the PR's code can read, by default also saved in .git/config by checkout
explain: Security Lab answers this exact question: the read/write GITHUB_TOKEN is in memory, and actions/checkout persists it on disk unless persist-credentials is false. npm install alone runs the PR author's install scripts.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: SBOMs: an ingredients list you can query when the alarm rings
question: What is a VEX document for?
options: Encrypting an SBOM
Replacing the lockfile
Signing artifacts
Stating whether a product is actually affected by a known vulnerability, so users can skip non-issues
explain: CISA describes VEX as a form of security advisory that indicates whether a product is affected. It pairs with SBOMs: the SBOM says the component is present; VEX says whether that matters.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: When a dependency is compromised: a response playbook
question: After the tj-actions compromise, a public repository finds the action ran during the window. Why is rotating secrets urgent even though no data went to an attacker's server?
options: It is not urgent; encoding protects them
Because GitHub automatically shares secrets with forks
Because the malicious code also deleted the repository
Because the secrets were printed, encoded, into workflow logs that anyone can read in a public repository
explain: The payload dumped runner memory into the job log, double base64-encoded, which is trivially reversible. Public repository logs are public, so every secret in that run must be considered exposed.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded
question: A lab plans each new model's pretraining mix with a fixed 10-trillion-token budget: every year it removes old human text to make room for the latest scrape, which is increasingly model-written. Which strategy from this lesson does that resemble most?
options: Accumulate, because the dataset is being refreshed
Replace, because older real data are discarded and model output takes their place
The fresh data loop, which MAD found safe in all cases
None, because a 10-trillion-token budget is too large for collapse
explain: Holding the budget fixed while swapping out human text for model output drifts toward the replace setting, where errors compound. Keeping the original real data and growing the corpus matches the accumulate results.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
question: A logger issues one `write` per 40-byte log line and handles 200,000 lines per second. Which change cuts syscall overhead the most?
options: Switch from write to pwrite
Accumulate lines in a 64 KiB buffer and write when it fills or on a short timer
Call fsync after every line so the kernel batches better
Open the log file with O_APPEND
explain: Overhead scales with the number of calls. Buffering 64 KiB packs about 1,638 lines per call, so 200,000 calls per second become about 122. pwrite (write at a given offset) and O_APPEND (every write lands at the end of the file) change semantics, not call count, and fsync, which forces data to disk, adds an even more expensive call per line. Keep a flush timer so a crash or a quiet period does not hold lines forever.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: MAP_SHARED, MAP_PRIVATE and copy-on-write
question: A program writes 100 MB into a MAP_SHARED file mapping, then the machine loses power before the program calls msync or munmap. What can you say about the file?
options: None of the writes are in the file
All of the writes are in the file, because shared mappings write through
The file is restored from the page cache on reboot
Any subset of the dirty pages may have reached the file
explain: The kernel writes dirty pages back whenever it chooses, so some may have reached the disk and others not, in no order you control. msync with MS_SYNC is how you force a range to disk and wait. This lack of ordering is why mmap-based databases still need a write-ahead log or shadow paging (as LMDB uses) to stay consistent.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Coordinated omission: the load tester stops looking when it hurts
question: A closed-loop benchmark with 50 connections reports p99 = 4 ms. During the run the server had a 2 second GC pause. Which is the most likely truth?
options: p99 is about 4 ms; the pause produced at most 50 slow samples and those are correctly counted
The true p99 for users arriving at a constant rate is likely far higher, because requests that should have been sent during the pause were never sent or measured
p99 is lower than 4 ms because the pause reduced load
Percentiles are unaffected by coordinated omission; only the mean is
explain: Each of the 50 connections recorded one long sample during the pause and then nothing until it resumed. A constant-rate workload would have issued many requests during those 2 seconds, each waiting out the pause. Those are missing, so the reported p99 is biased low. wrk2's README shows a 1.4 s pause turning p99 from 6.04 ms (uncorrected) into 1.27 s.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Why summing job durations overstates experience
question: Which single fact must be fixed before *current role* or *in the last 5 years* can be computed at all?
options: The candidate's time zone
The job titles of each role
The reference date that Present and now refer to
Whether the roles overlap
explain: Both questions are relative to a moment: current means containing that moment, and the last 5 years is a window ending at it. Without an explicit reference date the same resume gives different answers on different days.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Two ways to spend more compute on one prompt
question: A team samples 16 answers per question from a fixed model and keeps the one their reward model scores highest. In the proposer/verifier frame, what are they changing?
options: Only the verifier side: the proposal distribution is the same model sampled 16 times
Only the proposer: more samples means a better model
Both, because sampling at temperature changes the model's weights
Neither: this is training-time compute
explain: Best-of-N leaves the proposer untouched; each of the 16 samples comes from the same distribution. All the gain comes from selecting among them with a verifier. Changing the proposer means, for example, conditioning on previous attempts (revisions) or a longer reasoning trace.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
question: You fine-tuned a model like s1 and force 10 extra "Wait" continuations on every hard problem. Accuracy drops compared with 4. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model forgot its fine-tuning
Too many suppressed stops push it into repetitive loops or past the context window, so extra tokens stop adding useful reasoning
Appending "Wait" changes the model's weights
Budget forcing only works on easy problems
explain: s1 reports that scaling with budget forcing flattens and that suppressing the end-of-thinking delimiter too often leads to repetitive loops, while the context window bounds total length.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: One gradient step on a key-value loss is the delta rule
question: Which pair of choices turns the generic TTT layer into plain linear attention?
options: Linear model, batch gradient descent, W_0 = 0
Linear model, online gradient descent, W_0 = 0
Two-layer MLP, batch gradient descent, learned W_0
Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression with a softmax kernel
explain: Theorem 1 of the TTT paper: linear model, batch GD (all gradients at W_0) and W_0 = 0 give linear attention. Online GD gives the delta rule instead. The kernel-regression option is Theorem 2, which recovers softmax attention, not linear attention. Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression predicts a weighted average of stored values, weighted by a kernel's similarity between the query and each stored key.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans' three architectures, worked one segment at a time
question: In Titans (MAC) at test time, which part keeps changing its weights as the input streams in?
options: The persistent memory tokens
The attention projections W_Q, W_K, W_V
All three, since Titans fine-tunes itself at test time
The neural long-term memory M
explain: The paper is explicit: persistent memory parameters stay fixed because they encode task knowledge, the attention weights are fixed in-context learners, and only the long-term memory keeps learning (memorizing) at test time.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: One lock, many cores: why a shared slab cache stops scaling
question: Why did the original slab allocator get *slower* in total when going from 1 to 16 threads, rather than just staying flat?
options: Each thread ran its constructors twice
Contention made each lock handoff more expensive (cache line transfers, waiting, wakeups), so the serialized work itself took longer
The Starfire had only one memory controller
The slab layer disabled interrupts
explain: A flat ceiling assumes the critical section costs the same under load. Under contention the lock and freelist lines move between CPUs on every acquisition and waiters spin or sleep, so each serialized operation gets slower. The paper calls this increasingly pathological lock contention.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Today: thread caches, per-CPU caches and restartable sequences
question: In TCMalloc's rseq push (free), the code writes the object pointer into the slot and then stores the incremented `current`. Why is it fine if the thread is preempted between those two stores?
options: Preemption is disabled during free
The slot write is atomic
Nothing is published until the store to current commits; a restarted sequence just overwrites the same slot
The kernel replays the first store for it
explain: Only the final store to `current` makes the new object visible. If the thread is interrupted after writing the slot but before committing, the sequence restarts, recomputes the slot from the current header and rewrites it. TCMalloc's rseq notes describe exactly this: preempted sequences overwrite the deallocated object until one commits.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Stacking: let the rare thing rise to the top
question: Stacking scheduled task names across all machines gives 4,800 values that each appear once. What most likely went wrong?
options: The query needs a longer time range
Stacking does not work on scheduled tasks
The key contains a variable part (for example a user name or GUID) that should be normalised first
The fleet is heavily compromised
explain: A long tail made of thousands of singletons usually means the values differ only in an irrelevant part. Replace the variable part with a placeholder and stack again; the real outliers then stand out from a short tail.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Hunting in network data: rare, regular and unresolved
question: Host A's connection gaps to one address have a mean of 300 seconds and a standard deviation of 3 seconds. Host B's have a mean of 300 and a standard deviation of 240. Which is more likely automated check-ins, and what is each CV?
options: A: CV 0.01; B: CV 0.8. A is machine-like
Both are identical because the means are equal
B: CV 0.8 is more regular than A
explain: CV = standard deviation / mean: 3 / 300 = 0.01 for A and 240 / 300 = 0.8 for B. A connects almost exactly every five minutes, which is how scheduled software (benign or malicious) behaves. B varies like human activity. Next step for A: which process makes the connection, and is the destination rare?

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Measuring a hunt programme, and where to practise
question: A hunt is disproven: no ntds.dit copies on any domain controller in 90 days. What belongs in its write-up?
options: A statement that the network is secure
The hypothesis, data and time range checked, queries used, known-benign ntdsutil uses by named admins, any gaps found, and the detection or baseline it produced
Only the queries
Nothing; disproven hunts are not documented
explain: A disproven hunt is evidence that one behaviour did not occur in the data you had, for the period you checked. Writing down exactly what was checked, what was benign and what was missing lets the next hunter build on it, and keeps anyone from overstating it as 'the network is secure'.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Grading sources and information: the Admiralty code
question: A partner CERT (computer emergency response team) with a long record of accurate reporting shares a claim that no one else has reported and that fits what you already know. What grade fits best?
options: A1
F2
B5
A2
explain: The source has a history of complete reliability (A). The claim is logical and consistent but not independently confirmed, which is 2 (probably true), not 1. F would ignore the track record, and 5 would mean the claim is contradicted.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: STIX 2.1: threat intelligence as a graph
question: You have linked twelve intrusions by shared tooling and infrastructure but have no idea who is behind them. Which STIX object fits the cluster?
options: Threat Actor
Identity
Observed Data
Intrusion Set
explain: STIX defines an Intrusion Set as grouped adversarial behaviours and resources believed to be orchestrated by a single organisation, and allows activity to be attributed to it even when the Threat Actors are not known. A Threat Actor object asserts actual individuals or organisations.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Reading an intelligence product: CISA AA24-038A on Volt Typhoon
question: AA24-038A says conventional IOCs are 'generally lacking' for Volt Typhoon. What is the main reason?
options: The agencies chose not to publish indicators
The malware deletes itself after exactly 24 hours
IOCs are illegal to share across borders
The actors use built-in system tools, valid accounts and proxy networks of ordinary home and office routers, leaving few unique artefacts
explain: Living off the land means using tools already on the system and legitimate accounts, and the KV botnet routers give ordinary-looking source addresses. There is little malware to hash and little stable infrastructure to block, so behaviour detection and hunting carry the load.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Drawing the system: data flow diagrams and trust boundaries
question: A request travels from the Notes API to the database on another host inside your private network. Is that flow across a trust boundary?
options: No, because both are on the private network
No, because the API wrote the query itself
Usually yes: trust level changes between the app and data tiers, so the database should authenticate and limit the API
Only if the traffic is unencrypted
explain: A boundary is wherever the level of trust changes, not only the internet edge. Being on the same network is a location, not a trust decision. Encryption protects the flow but does not decide whether a boundary exists.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Ranking threats: risk, DREAD and why it fell out of favour
question: Two threats score 10 x 1 and 1 x 10 on probability times damage. What does that tell you?
options: They are equally urgent
Very little on its own: a frequent nuisance and a rare disaster look identical, so you need the reasons behind the scores
The first should be fixed first because it is more likely
The scoring was done wrong
explain: The Microsoft guide shows exactly this example to illustrate how the product works. Equal scores do not mean equal decisions; the reasons and the kind of harm matter.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Defence in depth and zero trust
question: Layers A, B and C each miss 20% of attacks independently. All three share one admin account that, if stolen, disables them all, with a 5% chance per year. Roughly what is the yearly chance of getting through?
options: About 5.8%
explain: Independent part: 0.2 cubed = 0.008. With the shared failure: 0.05 + 0.95 x 0.008 = 0.0576, about 5.8%. The shared account dominates; removing it matters more than a fourth layer.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: How Linux ranks nodes into tiers: abstract distance
question: Why does the kernel compute a single *top tier* boundary instead of letting every node promote to any faster node?
options: Because pages can only migrate between nodes in adjacent tiers
Because sysfs can only show one tier
Because the top tier is always exactly one node
Because memory near CPUs is where hot pages should end up; promoting between DRAM nodes is NUMA balancing's normal job, not tiering
explain: Tier promotion moves hot pages out of slow, CPU-less memory into memory that has CPUs. Between two DRAM nodes, ordinary NUMA balancing moves pages toward the CPU that uses them. The top-tier boundary separates the two cases (node_is_toptier()).

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Holt-Winters and ARIMA: models with trend and season
question: Which statement about ARIMA and exponential smoothing is correct according to FPP3?
options: SES is equivalent to ARIMA(0,1,1), but multiplicative exponential smoothing models have no ARIMA equivalent
ARIMA strictly contains every exponential smoothing model
ARIMA cannot model seasonality
Exponential smoothing models are all stationary
explain: Linear (additive) ETS models map to ARIMA forms, for example ETS(A,N,N) to ARIMA(0,1,1). Nonlinear ETS models have no ARIMA counterpart, and all ETS models are nonstationary while some ARIMA models are stationary. Seasonal ARIMA handles seasonality with seasonal lags and differencing.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: The TLS 1.3 handshake, message by message
question: Why does CertificateVerify sign a hash of the whole transcript rather than just the server's key share?
options: Hashing makes the signature shorter
Certificates cannot sign raw key shares
The transcript includes the client's offers and both key shares, so any tampering with the negotiation makes the signature fail
It lets the server skip the Finished message
explain: Signing everything the client sent and received binds the server's identity to this exact negotiation. An attacker who removed strong options from the ClientHello would change the transcript, and the signature would not verify.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Downgrade attacks: POODLE, BEAST, Logjam and the fixes
question: Why can a man in the middle not simply erase the DOWNGRD sentinel from the ServerHello random?
options: The random is encrypted
The server random is covered by the server's signature (ServerKeyExchange in TLS 1.2), so changing it breaks the signature check
The sentinel is checked by the CA
The sentinel is repeated in every record
explain: The randoms are inputs to what the server signs in a TLS 1.2 (EC)DHE handshake. Altering any byte invalidates the signature, which the client verifies with the certificate's key.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Certificate authorities, the CA/Browser Forum and ACME
question: Why does ACME's key authorization include a thumbprint of the client's account key rather than just the token?
options: It binds the proof to one ACME account, so a different account cannot reuse someone else's published token to get authorized
To make the file larger
Because the CA cannot generate random tokens
To encrypt the token
explain: The CA checks that the published value matches the token AND the account requesting the order. Proof of control is tied to a specific requester.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: HSTS, preloading and why key pinning fell out of favour
question: Why did Chrome remove HPKP?
options: Low adoption plus real risks: sites could lock out their own users, and attackers could set hostile pins; CT gave mis-issuance detection without those risks
Because it slowed down handshakes
Because CAs refused to support it
Because it only worked over HTTP/1.1
explain: Pinning's strength (hard rejection of unexpected keys) was also its danger. A mistake or a malicious pin could make a site unreachable for months.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Post-quantum key exchange: ML-KEM hybrids in TLS
question: A government agency records your TLS 1.3 traffic today, protected by plain X25519. Which threat does that create?
options: None, because TLS 1.3 has forward secrecy
A future quantum computer could solve X25519's discrete logarithm from the recorded key shares and decrypt the traffic (harvest now, decrypt later)
Only that your certificate could be forged today
Only metadata exposure
explain: Forward secrecy protects against later theft of long-term keys, not against breaking the ephemeral exchange itself. A quantum attacker breaks the recorded key shares directly, which is exactly what the hybrid prevents.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Tiled matmul: 2D pointer blocks, tl.dot and grouped ordering
question: A colleague removes other=0.0 from the A and B loads in the K loop because "the C store is masked anyway". When does this break?
options: Never, the store mask covers it
Only when M is not a multiple of BLOCK_SIZE_M
When K is not a multiple of BLOCK_SIZE_K, because undefined values in the last K tile get summed into every output
Only on AMD GPUs
explain: The store mask only drops rows and columns outside C. Garbage in the K dimension is not outside C: it is multiplied and accumulated into valid outputs. Masked K lanes must load 0.0, the neutral element of the sum in the dot product.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Attention masks for mixed text and image sequences
question: Why can Transfusion open up attention inside the image when Chameleon cannot?
options: Transfusion uses a larger context window
Chameleon images are smaller
Transfusion denoises all patches of an image at once, so every patch exists at every step, whereas Chameleon emits patches one by one
Transfusion has no text tokens inside images
explain: In a diffusion step all n patches (noisy versions of them) are in the sequence simultaneously, so a patch attending to a later patch reads something real. In token-by-token generation a later patch has not been sampled yet, so letting an earlier one see it during training would be a leak.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Building the image: micro-libraries, configuration and dead code
question: A unikernel serves files only from a RAM filesystem. Why does its image contain no block device driver, even though the Unikraft source tree has one?
options: The hypervisor provides block storage, so the driver is never needed
Block drivers are loaded as kernel modules at boot
Only components selected in the configuration or pulled in as dependencies are compiled and linked; nothing references the block layer
Dead code elimination removes all drivers by default
explain: Unikraft builds only selected micro-libraries and their dependencies. The paper notes the nginx image has no block subsystem because it only uses RamFS. There are no loadable modules in a unikernel.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Specializing further, and what you give up
question: An attacker finds a buffer overflow in a C web server. On a Linux VM they get code execution as the unprivileged web server user. What changes if the same server runs as a unikernel without memory protections?
options: They get code execution with full control of the VM, including raw packet I/O, with no privilege escalation step needed
Nothing: the hypervisor stops the exploit before it runs
The exploit fails because unikernels have no shell to spawn
They can immediately read the memory of other VMs on the host
explain: With one address space and one privilege level, the application is the kernel. NCC Group showed arbitrary packet I/O right after compromise. The hypervisor still confines the attacker to that VM, so other tenants remain protected unless the hypervisor itself is broken.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Why one vector distance is mostly a memory problem
question: Index A stores 1,536-d fp32 vectors. Index B stores 768-d int8 vectors. On a memory-bound scan, roughly how many more distances per second can B compute?
options: About the same, since both do one distance per vector
2x, because B has half the dimensions
8x, because B reads 768 bytes per vector instead of 6,144
4x, because int8 is a quarter of fp32
explain: Bytes per vector set the ceiling. A reads 1,536 x 4 = 6,144 bytes, B reads 768 x 1 = 768 bytes, a ratio of 8. Half the dimensions and a quarter of the bytes per dimension multiply.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Why verl splits the RL loop from the GPU programs
question: A researcher wants to add a second, greedy generation pass per prompt (as ReMax does) to compute a baseline. In verl's design, what has to change?
options: Every worker's SPMD program, because each must know when the extra pass happens
Only the controller loop: one more call to the existing generate_sequences with sampling turned off
The NCCL communicator setup between actor and critic
Nothing: verl decides which passes to run from the model architecture
explain: Stages are named calls on WorkerGroups, so a new dataflow is a new sequence of calls in the controller. The HybridFlow paper shows PPO, ReMax and Safe-RLHF (which adds a cost model that scores harmfulness) differing only in these few lines. In a multi-controller design the extra pass would have to be threaded through every model's program.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Backends, placement and running verl in practice
question: Your synchronous run's step time is dominated by a few very long responses, and the GPUs idle while waiting for them. Which verl option targets exactly this, and what does it cost?
options: Raise ppo_mini_batch_size; it costs more memory
Switch model_engine to megatron; it costs a checkpoint conversion
Lower rollout.n; it costs nothing
Use the one-step-off (or fully async) trainer with a separate rollout pool; training then uses samples from weights one step old
explain: The async trainers overlap generation with training on separate GPUs, so long-tail generation no longer stalls the update. The price is bounded staleness: data comes from the previous weights. Lowering n changes the algorithm, and mini-batch or engine changes do not touch the rollout tail.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Merging similar frames: MovieChat and MA-LMM memory banks
question: A 10-minute static lecture shot is followed by a 3-second cutaway, then the lecture again. With adjacent-similarity merging down to a small budget, what most likely happens?
options: The lecture frames collapse to few tokens while the cutaway survives as its own token
The cutaway is merged first because it is shortest
All frames are merged into one token immediately
The lecture frames are deleted and only the cutaway remains
explain: Near-identical lecture frames have the highest adjacent similarity, so they merge first. The cutaway has low similarity to both neighbors, so it is merged last, if at all. Merging spends the budget on change.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Tokenizing video and attending in space, then in time
question: Why might a spatial-only tokenizer (one frame at a time) give worse controllability than ST-ViViT?
options: Its codebook is necessarily smaller
Spatial attention is more expensive than temporal attention
It uses a causal mask in space
It cannot encode information about motion between frames into the tokens
explain: A per-frame encoder sees no other frames, so its tokens carry no motion context. The ST tokenizer's causal temporal layers let each frame's tokens include what happened before, which helps the downstream models predict and control change.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Turning an image into a sequence of patch tokens
question: You feed a 384x384 image to a ViT-B/16 (patch size stays 16). How long is the sequence the encoder processes?
options: 197, because the model was built for 224x224 and the extra pixels are cropped
577: a 24x24 grid of patches plus the CLS token
576: one token per patch, since the CLS token is only used at 224
1153, because the patch count scales with the image side length times 3 channels
explain: 384 / 16 = 24 patches per side, so 576 patches, plus CLS: 577. The transformer itself accepts any sequence length (up to memory); what does not fit is the table of 197 position embeddings, which is the subject of lesson 3.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train
question: You train LoRA (r = 16 on query and value) for ViT-B/16 and then merge the adapters with W = W0 + (alpha/r)BA. Compared with the original model, the merged model at inference has:
options: The same parameter count and the same latency
About 590K more parameters and a slightly slower forward pass
Half the parameters, since A and B replace W0
Lower accuracy, because merging rounds the update to low rank
explain: Merging adds BA into the existing matrices, so shapes are unchanged and so is the forward cost. The LoRA paper stresses this property: no additional inference latency compared with a fully fine-tuned model. The update was low rank during training too, so merging loses nothing.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: pi0: denoising a whole action chunk with flow matching
question: In the toy, you replace the 10 Euler steps with a single step of size 1 from tau = 0. What chunk comes out of the noise sample (0.25, 0.10)?
options: (0.6, 0.8), the R mode
(-0.6, -0.8), the L mode
(0.25, 0.10), unchanged
(0, 0), the average of the modes
explain: At tau = 0 both weights are 0.5, so v = (mean of modes) - x and x + v is the mean, (0, 0). One big step reproduces the regression failure; several small steps let the weights sharpen before the chunk moves far.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Vector quantization: snap each vector to its nearest code
question: A new encoder output is z = (0.1, -2.2). Using the toy codebook, which token id does it get?
explain: Squared distances: e5 gives 0.01 + 0.64 = 0.65, e3 gives 0.81 + 1.44 = 2.25 and e2 gives 1.21 + 1.44 = 2.65. The far-away code e5 wins, and that is exactly how a dead code can come back to life: an encoder output has to land near it.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Token budgets: bits per image, 1D tokenizers and early fusion
question: Chameleon's paper says its tokenizer struggles to reconstruct images containing a lot of text. What does that imply for the full model?
options: Nothing, because the transformer can learn the missing detail from more data
Its performance on text-heavy, OCR-like image tasks is upper-bounded by what the tokenizer keeps
Its text-only benchmarks will suffer
It must switch to continuous image features for those inputs
explain: The transformer only ever sees the token ids. Detail lost at tokenization cannot be recovered downstream, so the tokenizer caps OCR-heavy performance, as the paper states.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: KV cache layout and block sizes per backend
question: You serve an MLA model on Hopper with `--attention-backend FLASHMLA`, and you never passed `--block-size`. What block size does the KV cache use?
options: 16, the CacheConfig default, and FlashMLA pads each block
128, the largest size any MLA backend uses
It depends on max_model_len
64, because with no pinned size vLLM takes the backend's preferred size and FLASHMLA supports only 64
explain: Unpinned block sizes give way to the backend. `get_preferred_block_size` returns the default if it is supported and otherwise the smallest supported size, and FLASHMLA lists only 64. Had you pinned 16, FLASHMLA would have been rejected during selection.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Small text needs pixels: AnyRes tiling and dynamic resolution
question: A team switches from LLaVA-1.5 (one 336 px image) to an AnyRes model with up to 3 x 3 tiles plus a thumbnail. Accuracy on small text improves. What should they expect for cost?
options: Roughly the same, since the encoder is the same
Fewer tokens, because tiles are compressed
Exactly double
Up to about 10 times as many visual tokens per image (9 tiles plus 1 thumbnail), so higher latency and context use
explain: Each tile and the thumbnail is a full 336 px image of 576 tokens, so a 3 x 3 grid plus thumbnail is up to 10 x 576 = 5,760 visual tokens. Better reading is bought with tokens.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Herlihy's universal construction: announce, then help
question: Same construction, n = 4. P3 announces its cell when the newest cell has seq 9, then stalls. Under constant contention from the others, what seq will P3's cell get?
options: No bound, because P3 is stalled
explain: The cell after seq 9 is due to announce[(9 mod 4) + 1] = announce[2], so seq 10 is P2's. The cell after seq 10 is due to announce[(10 mod 4) + 1] = announce[3], so P3's cell becomes seq 11, helped in by whoever wins that slot.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Why learn the weather from 80 years of reanalysis
question: A startup says its MLWP model removes the need for any physics-based system in operations. What is the strongest objection?
options: MLWP models cannot run on GPUs
MLWP models need more compute than NWP per forecast
Each forecast starts from an analysis produced by NWP-based data assimilation, and training targets are NWP-based reanalysis
Reanalysis data is only available at 1 degree resolution
explain: The learned model replaces the forecast step, but both the initial state and the training data come from physics-based data assimilation. Inference is far cheaper than NWP, and ERA5 is available at 0.25 degrees.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Foundation models, hybrids, and where these models break
question: You need a 30-year climate simulation with prescribed sea-surface temperatures, and long-run stability matters more than peak 3-day accuracy. Which approach from this course fits best?
options: GraphCast rolled out for 30 years at 6-hour steps
Pangu-Weather's 24-hour model applied 10,950 times
NeuralGCM, the hybrid with a physics dynamical core and learned column physics
GenCast with 50 members
explain: NeuralGCM reports stable multi-decade runs tracking global mean temperature with prescribed SST. The pure MLWP models here were built and evaluated for medium-range (10 to 15 day) forecasting.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Mapping the application: entry points, roles and workflows
question: Why does the script replace numeric path segments with {id}?
options: To hide customer data from the report
Because ids are not sent to the server
Because WSTG forbids testing numeric parameters
So that many requests to the same endpoint count once, while marking it as carrying an object id
explain: Ids vary per request but the code path is the same. Collapsing them gives a true count of endpoints, and the {id} placeholder flags each one as a candidate for object-level authorization tests.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Testing sessions: tokens, cookie flags, fixation and logout
question: Which result of the logout replay test indicates a server-side session invalidation bug?
options: The browser shows the login page after logout
The logout request returns 302
The session cookie has the HttpOnly flag
The old session cookie, replayed after logout, still returns the account page
explain: The browser's view after logout proves nothing; only the server's response to the old token does. A 200 for the replayed token means the server-side session survived logout.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Chaining low findings into real impact
question: You found a self-XSS in your own profile and nothing else. How should you treat it in a bounty?
options: Report it as high severity because XSS is serious
Exploit it against real users to prove impact
Ignore XSS entirely
Note it, keep looking for a way to get it into another user's session (such as login CSRF), and report only if a plausible chain exists
explain: Self-XSS is P5 in the VRT because only you are affected. It becomes meaningful only with a step that delivers it to a victim. Testing that on real users is never acceptable; you demonstrate with two test accounts.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Coordinated disclosure: when and how to publish
question: Your report was marked Resolved on a HackerOne programme with the default disclosure setting, and the programme objects to publication. What now?
options: Publish anyway after 30 days
Publish on your own blog instead of HackerOne
Wait 7 days and publish
Do not publish; under the default setting an objection stops automatic disclosure, so discuss a timeline with the programme
explain: The default makes the report public within 30 days only if neither party objects. With an objection, you negotiate; the 180-day last resort applies only when a team does not respond at all, and only if its policy allows.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Cookies, sessions, and how Firesheep hijacked them in 2010
question: Why did Firesheep work against sites that already used HTTPS for their login page?
options: The passwords were stored without hashing
The session cookie was sent over plain HTTP on the pages after login
Firesheep could decrypt HTTPS traffic on open Wi-Fi
Their HTTPS certificates were invalid
explain: Only the login was encrypted. Every later request went over plain HTTP with the session cookie in the Cookie header, and on a shared network anyone could read and replay it. Firesheep never needed the password or any decryption.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: CORS with credentials, and the misconfigurations that leak data
question: Why is trusting `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null` dangerous?
options: Attackers can make a browser send Origin: null, for example from a sandboxed iframe or a data: URL
It is not dangerous; null means no origin can read
null disables the same-origin policy entirely
null is the origin of every localhost page
explain: Browsers send Origin: null from several unusual contexts, and an attacker controls some of them, such as a sandboxed iframe on their own page. Trusting null therefore trusts the attacker. PortSwigger recommends never allowlisting it.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: HTTPS, mixed content and HSTS: keeping the network out
question: An HTTPS page contains `` and ``. What do current browsers do?
options: Upgrade the image to HTTPS and block the script
Block both
Load both over HTTP and show a warning
Block the image and upgrade the script
explain: Images loaded via src are upgradable content: the browser tries the https URL instead. Scripts are blockable content, because a modified script would control the page, so the insecure request is not made at all.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: The map: what happens when you open one file on Windows
question: Ana's Word process opens a file. Whose identity does Windows check against the file's permissions?
options: The identity of whoever installed Word
The SIDs in the access token that Word inherited from Explorer, which came from Ana's sign-in
The computer's identity, because files belong to the computer
No identity: local files are always readable by local programs
explain: A process acts with its token. Word got a copy of Ana's token when Explorer started it, so the access check compares the file's ACL with Ana's user and group SIDs. Who installed the program does not matter.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: UAC and integrity levels: why admins do not run as admin
question: Ana is in Administrators with UAC on. Ana double-clicks a downloaded tool that does not ask for elevation. Which Token Elevation Type will its 4688 event show?
options: %%1936, a full token, because Ana is an admin
%%1938, a limited token
%%1937, an elevated token
No 4688 event is written for admins
explain: Programs started from Explorer inherit the filtered token unless they request elevation and the user approves. The limited token is type 3, logged as %%1938.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: The registry, Run keys and scheduled tasks: how programs come back
question: Which statement about RunOnce is correct according to Microsoft's documentation?
options: Its entries run at every sign-in forever
By default each value is deleted before its command runs, so it runs one time
It only works in Safe Mode
It requires a scheduled task to trigger it
explain: RunOnce values are deleted before the command runs by default (an exclamation mark prefix defers deletion until after). Run, without Once, repeats at every sign-in.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Sysmon and Microsoft Defender: deeper telemetry, built-in defence
question: A laptop's Defender log shows event 5001 at 03:12, followed by no detections all night. How should you read that?
options: Good news: no malware was detected
Suspicious: real-time protection was disabled, so the quiet night may mean nothing was being checked
Normal: 5001 is a daily heartbeat
It means Sysmon stopped
explain: 5001 means real-time protection was disabled. Silence after it is not evidence of safety. Tamper protection exists to stop exactly this.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: First look at domains and Active Directory
question: Maersk's recovery depended on one domain controller that was offline during the attack. What defensive practice does that point to?
options: Keeping RDP open on DCs for faster recovery
Keeping offline, unreachable backups of Active Directory
Running more domain controllers on the same network
Disabling Kerberos
explain: Every online DC replicated with or was reachable by the malware. Only an offline copy survived. Offline backups of AD are a core resilience control.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Why a captured handshake allows offline password guessing
question: Why is a network named after the router's factory default slightly easier to attack than a uniquely named one, even with the same passphrase strength?
options: Default names disable encryption
The SSID is the PBKDF2 salt, so work precomputed for that common name can be reused across all networks with that name
Default names use WEP
It is not; the SSID has no effect on the PMK
explain: The PMK depends on both passphrase and SSID. A shared SSID across many networks lets an attacker amortise precomputation, the problem salts were meant to prevent.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Rogue access points, evil twins and how enterprises find them
question: A sensor hears a BSSID that is in your inventory, but it now advertises CorpNet as an open network instead of WPA3-Enterprise. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The AP was upgraded
An attacker is spoofing that AP's BSSID to look legitimate, but cannot copy the Enterprise authentication
Normal roaming behaviour
A KRACK attack in progress
explain: Copying a MAC address is trivial; copying the RADIUS server's certificate and keys is not. A security-mode mismatch on a known BSSID is a classic impersonation signal.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Android: UID sandbox, SELinux, verified boot and Play Protect
question: App A and app B on Android are both malicious and collude. App A makes its private files world-readable so B can read them. On an Android 13 device, where A targets API 33, what stops this?
options: The per-app SELinux sandbox for apps targeting API 28+, which prevents apps from making their data world-accessible
Play Protect deletes the files
Verified boot
Nothing; world-readable means everyone
explain: AOSP: since Android 9, non-privileged apps targeting API 28+ run in individual SELinux sandboxes, which 'prevents apps from making their data world accessible'. Mandatory access control overrides the owner's choice.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Managing fleets: MDM, BYOD and SIM swap defences
question: An employee enrolls a personal iPhone through account-driven User Enrollment. Which action is outside what the organisation can do?
options: Configure the corporate Wi-Fi with a pinned CA
Read the user's personal iCloud photos
Remove its managed data
Install a managed work app
explain: Apple's design: with User Enrollment, IT can manage only the organisation's accounts, settings and information, never the user's personal account. Selective removal of managed data is in scope; personal content is not.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Why a pool needs more than one shared queue
question: Which workload gains the most from work stealing over static per-worker queues?
options: Millions of identical 1 ms tasks dealt evenly to workers
A single long task that cannot be split
Tasks that each hold a global lock for their whole run
A recursive divide-and-conquer job whose subproblems vary wildly in size
explain: Stealing fixes imbalance. Evenly dealt identical tasks have none, one unsplittable task cannot be shared, and a global lock serializes everything anyway. Uneven recursive work is exactly where idle workers find something to steal.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Parking idle workers without lost wakeups or thundering herds
question: A pool notifies a parked worker on every single push. A burst of 1,000 tasks arrives on one worker with 15 workers parked. What is the main problem?
options: Tasks are executed twice
All 15 workers can be woken at once and pile onto the same victim queue, and many go back to sleep empty-handed
Tasks are lost because the futex only wakes one thread
Nothing; more wakeups always help
explain: That is the thundering herd the Tokio 0.1 scheduler suffered. Waking only when nobody is searching, and letting each successful searcher wake the next, brings workers online one at a time as they find work.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Tuning the cooldown: length, shape, floor and data
question: OLMo 2 runs three 50B-token anneals of the same 7B checkpoint on the same mix and averages them. Why can averaging these work, when averaging two independently pretrained models usually would not?
options: Averaging always works for any two models of the same architecture
Each anneal uses a different LR, so averaging gives the best LR
The three anneals start from the same weights and stay close to each other, so their average lies in the same low-loss basin and cancels part of each run's data-order noise
The average is only used for evaluation; the released model is the first anneal
explain: The ingredients share a starting point and differ only by data order, so they stay near one another and averaging cancels part of each run's noise, the same idea as checkpoint averaging in lesson 7. Wortsman et al., whose model soups OLMo 2 cites, observed that models fine-tuned from the same pretrained weights often lie in a single low-error basin; nothing guarantees that for independently trained networks.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: Where the copies go in a read and write loop
question: How many CPU copies per byte does mmap + write leave, and why not zero?
options: Zero, because the mapped pages are the page cache
Two, because mmap copies the file into anonymous memory
One, because write() must copy from the user pointer into the socket buffer
One, because mmap copies the file on the first page fault
explain: mmap removes the page cache to user copy: the mapping points at page cache pages. But write() is a copying interface. Once it returns you may modify the buffer, so the kernel copies the bytes into the socket buffer during the call.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Classifying with labels chosen at inference time
question: A support-ticket router uses an NLI zero-shot classifier with 6 labels. Product asks for a 7th label, refund request. What is the minimum change?
options: Add a 7th output unit to the model and fine-tune it on refund tickets
Append the string refund request to the label list, then re-check accuracy on a small labeled set
Retrain the NLI model on MNLI with refund examples added
Nothing: the model will start emitting the new label on its own
explain: The label set is an input at inference time, so adding a label is a one-line change. The model is never retrained. You should still re-check accuracy, because the new label competes with the existing ones and may steal their mass. The model cannot emit a label you did not pass in.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Evaluating zero-shot classifiers and choosing thresholds
question: You have 200,000 product descriptions and 5,000 category labels, and need one pass over them tonight. Which family fits the budget best?
options: NLI cross-encoder, because it is the most accurate
Embedding similarity: 205,000 encoder passes with cached label vectors, versus a billion pairs for NLI
An LLM call per (description, label) pair
Contextual calibration alone
explain: NLI needs one pass per pair: 200,000 x 5,000 = 1 billion. Embeddings need one pass per description plus one per label, 205,000 in total, and label vectors can sit in a vector index for fast lookup. You can still rerank the top few candidates per item with a slower scorer.
